subject: maths
title: Mean, median, mode and range
summary: Learn to find the mean, median, mode and range of a set of data, and to choose the average that best describes the data when there is an outlier.
body:
When someone says "the average Year 7 student sleeps about nine hours a night", they are using one number to describe a whole group. Sports stats, school reports and weather records all use averages like this. In this lesson you will learn the three kinds of average — the mean, the median and the mode — and the range, which tells you how spread out the data is.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can find the mean, median, mode and range of a set of data, and decide which average best describes the data.

## Before you start

You need to add and divide whole numbers (from *Multiplying and dividing whole numbers (Year 7)*), put numbers in order, and work with decimals (from *Rounding decimals (Year 7)*).

**Warm-up**

1. Work out 12 + 15 + 9 + 4. *(Answer: 40)*
2. Work out 40 ÷ 4. *(Answer: 10)*

## Think of it like this

### Sharing lollies fairly

Four friends have 12, 15, 9 and 4 lollies. If they put them all in one bowl (40 lollies) and share them equally, each gets 40 ÷ 4 = 10. That "fair share" is the **mean**: add everything up, then share it out equally.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* lollies come in whole numbers, but a mean can be a decimal — the mean number of pets might be 1.4, even though no one owns 1.4 pets.

## Key ideas

### Measures of centre

A **measure of centre** is one number that describes the "middle" or typical value of a set of data. There are three:

### The mean

The **mean** is what most people call "the average".

`mean = sum of all the values ÷ number of values`

The mean uses every value, so one very large or very small value can drag it a long way.

![A column graph of the lollies four friends have: 12, 15, 9 and 4. A dashed line at 10 shows the mean — the level every bar would be if the lollies were shared equally](/diagrams/y7/maths/mean-median-mode-and-range-mean.svg)

### The median

The **median** is the middle value when the data is in order from smallest to largest.

- With an **odd** number of values, there is one middle value.
- With an **even** number of values, there are two middle values — the median is halfway between them (add them and divide by 2).

A quick way to find the middle position: for n values, the median is at position (n + 1) ÷ 2. For 7 values, that is position 4.

### The mode

The **mode** is the value that occurs most often. A set of data can have one mode, two modes (**bimodal**), or no mode if every value appears the same number of times. The mode is the only average you can use for categorical data, like favourite colour.

### The range

The **range** measures **spread**, not centre:

`range = largest value − smallest value`

A small range means the values are close together; a large range means they are spread out.

### Outliers and choosing an average

An **outlier** is a value much bigger or smaller than the rest. An outlier pulls the mean towards it but hardly changes the median. So:

- Use the **mean** when there are no outliers (it uses all the data).
- Use the **median** when there is an outlier, like one very high house price.
- Use the **mode** for the most popular choice, or for categories.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 7, 3, 9, 3, 8.

Step 1: order the data — so you can find the middle and the extremes: 3, 3, 7, 8, 9.
Step 2: mean — add the values and divide by how many there are: (3 + 3 + 7 + 8 + 9) ÷ 5 = 30 ÷ 5 = **6**.
Step 3: median — there are 5 values, so the middle is position (5 + 1) ÷ 2 = 3: the median is **7**.

![Five cards in order: 3, 3, 7, 8, 9, labelled 1st to 5th. The 3rd card, 7, is highlighted as the middle](/diagrams/y7/maths/mean-median-mode-and-range-ex1.svg)

Step 4: mode — 3 appears twice, more than any other value: the mode is **3**.
Step 5: range — largest minus smallest: 9 − 3 = **6**.
Check: 5 values × mean 6 = 30, which matches the sum ✓

### Example 2

The numbers of push-ups six students did were 14, 9, 12, 20, 11, 16. Find the median, the mean (to 1 decimal place) and the range.

Step 1: order the data: 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 20.
Step 2: there are 6 values (even), so the two middle values are the 3rd and 4th: 12 and 14 — because there is no single middle value.
Step 3: median = (12 + 14) ÷ 2 = 26 ÷ 2 = **13** — halfway between the middle two.

![Six cards in order: 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 20. The 3rd and 4th cards, 12 and 14, are highlighted as the two middle values](/diagrams/y7/maths/mean-median-mode-and-range-ex2.svg)

Step 4: mean = (9 + 11 + 12 + 14 + 16 + 20) ÷ 6 = 82 ÷ 6 = 13.666… ≈ **13.7**.
Step 5: range = 20 − 9 = **11**.
Check: the median (13) is not one of the data values — that is fine with an even number of values.

### Example 3

Jess's mean mark on 4 tests is 85. Her first three marks were 82, 90 and 78. What did she get on the fourth test?

Step 1: find the total of all 4 marks — because mean × number of values = sum: 85 × 4 = 340.
Step 2: add the three marks you know: 82 + 90 + 78 = 250.
Step 3: subtract to find the missing mark: 340 − 250 = **90**.
Check: (82 + 90 + 78 + 90) ÷ 4 = 340 ÷ 4 = 85 ✓

### Example 4

Six friends counted how many hours of sport they played last week: 2, 3, 3, 4, 3, 25. Which average describes this data best?

Step 1: mean = (2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 25) ÷ 6 = 40 ÷ 6 ≈ 6.7 hours.
Step 2: median — order the values: 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 25. The middle two are 3 and 3, so the median is **3** hours.
Step 3: compare — 25 is an outlier that drags the mean up to 6.7, which is more than five of the six friends played.
Step 4: so the **median (3 hours)** describes a typical friend best.

![A dot plot of hours of sport: dots at 2, 3, 3, 3, 4 and one far away at 25, marked outlier. A dashed line shows the median at 3 and another shows the mean at about 6.7, to the right of almost all the dots](/diagrams/y7/maths/mean-median-mode-and-range-ex4.svg)

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting to order the data before finding the median.** The middle of an unordered list means nothing. Fix: always write the values in order first.
- **Dividing by the wrong number for the mean.** Fix: count how many values there are (including any zeros) and divide by that.
- **Giving the range as "3 to 9".** The range is one number: 9 − 3 = 6. Fix: subtract smallest from largest.
- **Mixing up the mode and its frequency.** If 3 appears twice, the mode is 3, not 2. Fix: the mode is a data value.
- **Picking the middle two for an odd count, or one value for an even count.** Fix: use (n + 1) ÷ 2 to find the position.

## Tips to remember

- **"Hey diddle diddle, the median's the middle; you add and divide for the mean. The mode is the one that appears the most, and the range is the difference between."** A well-known rhyme.
- **Median sounds like "medium"** — the one in the middle.
- **Mode = "most"** — both start with "mo".
- **Range = "from the top to the bottom"** — like a mountain range from peak to valley.
- **Outlier? Use the median.** One giant value can't push the middle around.

## Key terms

- **Mean** — the sum of the values divided by the number of values.
- **Median** — the middle value when the data is in order.
- **Mode** — the value that occurs most often.
- **Range** — the largest value minus the smallest value.
- **Measure of centre** — a single value that describes the typical value of a data set.
- **Spread** — how far apart the values are.
- **Outlier** — a value much larger or smaller than the rest.
- **Bimodal** — having two modes.

## Summary

- Mean = sum ÷ number of values; it uses every value but is pulled by outliers.
- Median = middle value of the ordered data; with an even count, halfway between the middle two.
- Mode = most common value; it can be used for categorical data.
- Range = largest − smallest; it measures spread, not centre.
- If there is an outlier, the median usually describes the data better than the mean.

questions.prompt: The column graph shows the goals scored by four players: 4, 8, 6 and 2. Find the mean.
questions.explanation: Add the values (4 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 20) and divide by how many there are (4): 20 ÷ 4 = 5. The answer 20 is the sum — you still need to divide.
steps: Divide the sum by the count: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 20 is the sum. Divide it by the number of values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 8 − 2 = 6 is the range. For the mean, add all the values and divide.
mistakes.D: Step 2: count again — there are 4 values, not 3.

questions.prompt: Find the median of the numbers on the five cards: 5, 9, 2, 7, 4.
questions.explanation: In order the values are 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle one is 5. The answer 2 is the middle of the list before it was put in order.
steps: There are 5 values, so the middle is the 3rd one: 5.

mistakes.A: Step 1: put the values in order first — 2 is only in the middle of the unordered list.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 9 − 2 = 7 is the range. The median is the middle value of the ordered list.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 27 ÷ 5 = 5.4 is the mean. The median is the middle value once ordered.

questions.diagram_alt: Five number cards in this order: 5, 9, 2, 7, 4

questions.explanation: 3 appears three times, more than any other value, so the mode is 3. The value 6 appears only twice.
steps: Count how often each value appears: 3 → three times, 6 → twice, 5 and 8 → once.
The mode is the value that appears most often: 3.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 6 appears twice, but 3 appears three times. Count each value carefully.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 8 is the largest value. The mode is the most common value, not the biggest.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 5 is the median (the middle once ordered). The mode is the most common value.

questions.prompt: The number line shows the values 13, 21, 17, 8 and 26. Find the range.
questions.explanation: The largest value is 26 and the smallest is 8, so the range is 26 − 8 = 18. The answer 13 uses the last and first values in the list, not the largest and smallest.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 26 − 13 = 13 uses the first value in the list. The smallest value is 8.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 17 is the median. The range is the largest minus the smallest.
mistakes.D: Step 3: the range is a single number — subtract the smallest from the largest.

questions.explanation: In order: 7, 9, 11, 15. With 4 values, the median is halfway between the middle two: (9 + 11) ÷ 2 = 10. The answer 11 comes from using the middle two of the unordered list (7 and 15).
steps: There are 4 values (even), so take the middle two: 9 and 11.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you used the middle two of the unordered list (7 and 15). Order the values first.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 42 ÷ 4 = 10.5 is the mean. The median uses only the middle two values.
mistakes.D: Step 2: with an even number of values there are two middle values — find halfway between 9 and 11.

questions.prompt: The column graph shows how many books five students read last month. What is the mean?
questions.explanation: The sum is 0 + 3 + 5 + 0 + 2 = 10, and there are 5 values, so the mean is 10 ÷ 5 = 2. The answer 3.33 leaves out the two zeros — but they are real answers and must be counted.
steps: Count the values, including the zeros: 5.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 0 is the mode (it appears twice). The mean is the sum divided by the count.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the zeros are students too — divide by 5, not 3.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 10 is the sum. Divide it by the number of students.

questions.prompt: The mean of five numbers is 14. Four of the numbers are 12, 15, 10 and 18. What is the fifth number?
questions.explanation: Five numbers with mean 14 add to 5 × 14 = 70. The four known numbers add to 55, so the fifth is 70 − 55 = 15. The answer 14 just repeats the mean; the missing number does not have to equal the mean.
steps: Total of all five numbers = mean × count = 14 × 5 = 70.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 55 is the total of the four known numbers. Subtract it from the total of all five.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 55 ÷ 4 is the mean of the four known numbers. Find the total of all five first: 14 × 5.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the mean is 14, but the missing number can be different. Work out the total with 14 × 5.

questions.prompt: The column graph shows the prices five houses in a street sold for: $480 000, $2 100 000, $420 000, $510 000 and $450 000. Which measure best describes a typical price, and what is it?
questions.explanation: The $2 100 000 house is an outlier that drags the mean up to $792 000, more than four of the five prices. The median, $480 000, is not affected by the outlier, so it describes a typical house better.
steps: Look for an outlier: $2 100 000 is far above the rest.
An outlier pulls the mean, so use the median.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the mean is pulled up by the $2 100 000 outlier — four of the five houses cost less than $792 000.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the range tells you the spread, not a typical price.
mistakes.D: Step 3: $420 000 is the middle of the unordered list. Put the prices in order first.

questions.prompt: The numbers 6, 8 and 10 have a mean of 8. A fourth number, 16, is added. What is the new mean?
questions.explanation: The new sum is 6 + 8 + 10 + 16 = 40, and there are now 4 numbers, so the mean is 40 ÷ 4 = 10. The answer 12 averages the old mean (8) with 16, which treats 16 as if it counted the same as all three old numbers together.

mistakes.A: Step 1: adding a number bigger than the mean pushes the mean up. Find the new sum and divide.
mistakes.C: Step 1: don't just average 8 and 16 — add all four numbers, then divide by 4.
mistakes.D: Step 2: there are now 4 numbers, so divide 40 by 4, not by 3.

questions.prompt: Ali's first four quiz scores are 12, 15, 9 and 14. What must he score on the fifth quiz so that his mean for all five quizzes is exactly 13?
questions.explanation: For a mean of 13 over 5 quizzes, the total must be 5 × 13 = 65. His first four add to 50, so he needs 65 − 50 = 15. The answer 2 uses 4 quizzes (4 × 13 = 52) instead of 5.
steps: A mean of 13 over 5 quizzes needs a total of 5 × 13 = 65.
His first four scores add to 12 + 15 + 9 + 14 = 50.

mistakes.A: Step 1: scoring 13 keeps his mean below 13, because his first four only average 12.5. Find the total needed: 5 × 13.
mistakes.B: Step 1: there will be 5 quizzes, not 4 — the total needed is 5 × 13.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 65 is the total needed for all five quizzes. Subtract the 50 he already has.

questions.prompt: Three whole numbers have a median of 6, a mean of 7 and a range of 7. What is the largest of the three numbers?
questions.explanation: The numbers add to 3 × 7 = 21, and the middle one is 6, so the smallest and largest add to 15 and differ by 7: they are 4 and 11. The answer 13 just adds the median and the range, which would need the smallest number to be 6.
steps: The median is the middle number, 6, so smallest + largest = 21 − 6 = 15.
Two numbers that add to 15 and differ by 7 (the range) are 4 and 11, so the largest is 11.

mistakes.B: Step 3: median + range only works if the smallest number equals the median. Find two numbers that add to 15 and differ by 7.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 21 is the sum of all three numbers, not the largest one.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 4 is the smallest of the three numbers. The question asks for the largest.

questions.prompt: A class of 10 students has a mean test mark of 60. A new student joins and scores 82 on the same test. What is the new class mean?
questions.explanation: The 10 students scored 10 × 60 = 600 marks in total. With the new student it is 682 marks shared among 11 students: 682 ÷ 11 = 62. The answer 71 averages 60 and 82, as if the new student counted as much as the other ten together.

mistakes.A: Step 1: one student can't count as much as ten. Find the total marks first: 10 × 60.
mistakes.B: Step 3: there are now 11 students, so divide by 11, not 10.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a score above the mean pushes the mean up. Add 82 to the total and divide again.
